title: PySpark persist() placement for a frequently mutating df
question:
Persist() is helpful when the same dataframe is used repeatedly in the code.

But what about cases where transformations are on top of each other?:

a = spark.createDataFrame(data)
trigger action on a

b = a # Perform operations on a
trigger action on b

c = b # Perform operations on b
trigger action on c

d = c # Perform operations on c
trigger action on d

I would be tempted to persist() each dataframe before each trigger; however, persisting that many times would be time-consuming. Another option would be to persist on a midpoint, for example, b, so that at least the computation for c and d is faster.

In either case, it seems that the benefit we receive from persist() drops greatly compared to when running analysis tasks on just a.

Where would you place persist() for use cases where actions need to be frequently called on dataframes, which always build on top of previous ones?

An example case in which I previously faced this problem was a pipeline that applies multiple cleaning operations on a dataframe. After each cleaning step, we had to trigger an action to check the effect on the data (show or write).

EDIT: To clarify, the opeartions applied before each actions, are a mix of filterings, sorting, addition and modification of columns.
answer:
Not sure what kind of transformations you applied on each step, here is my two cents:

  1. Will persisting prevent file scanning again? I saw some pipelines which count the number and then write the data to the storage after transformation using the same dataframe without any persisting. When execution plan was checked, it triggered the same file scanning process. File scanning could be very slow, especially when your storage is remote, or underlying data is fragmented (many small files), or inefficient data partition or other reasons. Also, data deserialization by Spark executor also takes time. If you know that your action will trigger the process which starting from file scanning and you have sufficient resources, persisting might be a good choice for you to optimize the performance.

  2. Will the transformation trigger data shuffling? One of the most expensive things in Spark is data shuffling, as it involves data network transfer, serialization / deserialization overhead, CPU overhead etc. If you know that all transformations are narrow transformation, for example filter() or withColumn() with if condition to create new column, before calling the action, then I think you can skip the persisting. If you know that a data shuffling will be involved, then persisting could be a way to improve the performance.

------

Edit: 1 on 2025-09-17

To or not to persist the dataframe depends on the context.

Ideally, it will be faster if we can cache (i.e. persist in the memory only) the dataframe. However, as you've already known that persisting so many time would be time-consuming, as samkart has already explained to you why persisting is not always faster. Even you can cache the data in the memory, it might still be evicted if the storage usage is above a certain threshold (https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/tuning.html#memory-management-overview).

To answer your question, it depends. Although calling action on D might trigger the transformation starting from A, if I know that only narrow transformations exists between actions, and resources are limited in the application that I can't fully cache the dataframe in the memory, I would probably not to persist at a middle point, as I doubt how much it can optimized by using persisting, also Spark execution engine will optimize the query plan.

But if your transformation from a to b filter out 99% of your original data and this step takes 80% of your pipeline running time, that's a different story.
